To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) phenotypic errors (transcription errors) can promote the evolution of more stable proteins; 2) the increased stability of these proteins enables them to better tolerate destabilizing mutations (transcriptional or genetic errors); 3) the stabilized protein variants are more resistant to antibiotics; and 4) the stabilized variants are also more tolerant of genetic mutations.

(a) an increase in transcription errors promotes the evolution of higher enzyme expression and of more stable variants; (b) the stabilized variants are more resistant to genetic mutations; (c) the stabilized variants show a distinct advantage under transcriptional error conditions, although under normal conditions they confer resistance similar to wild type; and (d) the stabilized variants increase enzyme resistance by decreasing the deleterious effect of destabilizing mutations that occur as a result of transcriptional errors.
phenotypic mutations can promote the evolution of protein stability, expression levels and tolerance to genetic changes.
